exam: A 6‑year‑old presents with sudden weakness of the left arm and facial droop. What is the first investigation? — Look for polio; order a nerve conduction study or CSF analysis if available.
A child with HIV has progressive limb weakness. What drug should be avoided due to neurotoxicity? — Trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole (can worsen neuropathy).
A 4‑year‑old shows muscle wasting but reflexes are normal. What is the next step? — Repeat examination after 1–2 weeks; early LMN may have preserved reflexes.
A child with suspected TB meningitis has normal CSF protein. What explains this? — Early disease may have normal protein; repeat CSF after 1 week.
A child with facial weakness cannot close the eye. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Lower motor neuron facial palsy (Bell's palsy or infectious).
A child with severe pain in the limbs and absent reflexes is found to have hypokalaemia. What is the management? — Correct potassium and monitor for respiratory compromise.
ai.title: Lower Motor Neuron Disorders
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Lower motor neuron (LMN) lesions cause muscle wasting, fasciculations, reduced tone and absent reflexes. In children, common causes are infections, metabolic disorders and trauma. Rapid assessment and targeted investigations guide treatment.

b: Clinical exam: weakness, atrophy, fasciculations, reduced tone, absent reflexes
sections.p: LMN refers to the nerve cells in the spinal cord or cranial nerve nuclei that directly innervate skeletal muscle. Damage leads to weakness, atrophy, fasciculations and loss of reflexes.

t.b: Identify weakness, atrophy, fasciculations, reduced tone and absent reflexes

sections.p: Severity is staged by the extent of weakness and functional loss. The Medical Research Council (MRC) grading (0–5) is commonly used.

b: Infections: polio, HIV‑associated neuropathy, TB meningitis, malaria‑related neuropathy
Metabolic: hypoglycaemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, thiamine deficiency
Trauma: birth injury, penetrating wounds, spinal cord injury
Congenital: spinal muscular atrophy, congenital myopathies
sections.p: In low‑resource settings the most common LMN causes are infections, metabolic derangements and trauma.

b: Absent or reduced deep tendon reflexes
sections.p: Children present with sudden or progressive weakness, often asymmetric. Facial weakness includes forehead involvement, leading to inability to close the eye. Reflex loss is a key sign.
Investigations are guided by the suspected cause and available resources.
Urgent red flags include respiratory muscle weakness, severe pain, rapid progression, or signs of systemic infection.

b: Treat infection: antitubercular therapy, antiretroviral therapy, antimalarials
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide supportive care and monitor for complications. Pharmacologic choices are limited by availability and safety.
Regular follow‑up to assess recovery, prevent complications and monitor for recurrence. Prevention focuses on infection control and nutritional support.

b: Metabolic myopathies: exercise intolerance, normal reflexes
sections.p: Upper motor neuron lesions, myasthenia gravis and metabolic myopathies can mimic LMN signs.
Normal reflexes can be seen in early LMN disease; CSF protein may be normal in early polio.
